extracted.intended_audience: students, instructors, and readers of Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis (people working through the text or checking errata)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of comments and errata for Walter Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis pointing out missing hypotheses, ambiguous problem statements, measure-theoretic caveats, and minor typographical errors to watch for when reading or doing exercises from the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses stated before theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hypotheses to theorems are stated a bit before the theorems rather than in the theorems themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: check surrounding text for assumptions that are not repeated in the theorem statement itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing common theorem names
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theorems are not given their common name. For example Theorem 7.25 is the Arzela-Ascoli theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize standard theorem names even when Rudin does not label them; this helps connect to known results and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit nonemptiness of metric spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: When Rudin says X is a metric space, he almost always means that X is nonempty without stating it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume metric spaces are intended to be nonempty unless the empty case is explicitly discussed; check proofs that use existence of points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check domains in exercise statements
rubrics_metrics.description: In chapter 7, problem 4, the sum doesn't make sense when x = -1/n^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the domain of variables in problem statements; if ambiguous, restrict (e.g. work out the problem for x ≥ 0) or interpret the intended domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructed functions vs. subsequential limits
rubrics_metrics.description: In problem 13 (ch.7), in hint part (ii) Rudin constructs an f, but that will not be the f that the final subsequence converges to. In (iv) we only conclude that there is a subsequence that converges everywhere, but its limit could be different from the constructed f at countably many points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that a function constructed in a hint may differ from the limit of a subsequence; consider renaming functions (e.g. use g) to avoid confusion. As an exercise, find sequences where the constructed f cannot be the subsequential limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiability of inverse of increasing function
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudin states that if E is strictly increasing and differentiable, then its inverse is also (differentiable), but does not indicate where this is proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact requires supporting results (e.g. exercise 2 on page 114) or a direct proof. Do not treat it as entirely trivial; either cite the exercise or provide a direct proof to obtain the derivative of the inverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure-theoretic claims need finite-measure caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: On page 309, remark part b: the claim follows directly from the definition only if μ(A) < ∞. It is slightly harder for sets of infinite measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sets of infinite measure, handle by decomposing A into finite-measure pieces (e.g. A_j = A ∩ [j,j+1)) and approximate each piece (find G_j with μ(G_j \ A_j) < ε 2^{-|j|-2}). Explicitly address infinite-measure cases rather than assuming finiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurability often omitted before integration
rubrics_metrics.description: All over chapter 11, Rudin sometimes forgets to mention 'measurable' for a function and then integrates it. You should think, whenever you see ∫_E f dμ, Rudin assumes f is measurable. The hypothesis of measurable is missing for example in exercises 1, 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check (or assume and verify) measurability before integrating; add the measurable hypothesis explicitly when working exercises or proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: L(μ) and L^2(μ) require a.e. identification
rubrics_metrics.description: In exercise 11 (p.333) and remark after Theorem 11.42 (p.329), ℒ(μ) and ℒ^2(μ) are metric spaces only when functions are identified if they are equal almost everywhere. So really it's the set of those equivalence classes in ℒ(μ) and ℒ^2(μ) that are complete metric spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat L-spaces as spaces of equivalence classes modulo a.e. equality when discussing metrics and completeness; make this identification explicit in statements and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor typographical errata
rubrics_metrics.description: On page 213, equation (16) there is a missing vertical bar in the numerator. On page 313, equation (49) the sum is over i not n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert for small typographical mistakes (missing symbols, wrong summation index) and correct them when reading or using the text.
